title: That men are justly punished for being obstinate in the defence of a fort that is not in reason to be defended
paragraphs: Valour has its bounds as well as the other virtues, which, once crossed, the next step is into the territory of vice. So that, having too large a share of this heroic virtue, unless a man knows its limits very precisely (and on the borderline they are very hard to make out), he may easily, without realising it, run into temerity, obstinacy, and folly. From this it is that we have derived the custom, in times of war, of punishing even with death those who stubbornly defend a place that, by the rules of war, is not tenable; otherwise men would be so emboldened by the hope of impunity that not a henroost but would resist and try to hold up an army.

The Constable Monsieur de Montmorency, having at the siege of Pavia been ordered to cross the Ticino and take up his quarters in the Faubourg St Antonio, was held up by a tower at the end of the bridge so stubborn as to endure a battery; for which he hanged every man he found inside. And again, accompanying the Dauphin in his expedition over the Alps, and taking the castle of Villano by assault, where all inside had been put to the sword by the fury of the soldiers, the governor and his ensign alone excepted, he had these two trussed up too for the same reason. So also did Captain Martin du Bellay, then governor of Turin, with the governor of San Buono, in that same country, all of whose people had been cut to pieces at the taking of the place.

But since the strength or weakness of a fortress is always measured against the forces attacking it — a man might reasonably enough despise two culverins but would be a madman to face a battery of thirty cannon — and since the greatness of the prince commanding the field, his reputation, and the respect owed him are also weighed in, there is a danger that the scales tip too far in that direction. It may happen that a man becomes so impressed with himself and his power that, thinking it unreasonable for any place to dare to shut its gates against him, he puts everything to the sword wherever he meets resistance, as long as his fortune holds. So in the fierce and arrogant forms of summoning towns and declaring war, savouring of barbarian pride and insolence, that are still in use among the eastern princes — and that their successors to this day retain and practise. And in that part of the world where the Portuguese subdued the Indians, they found some states where it was a universal and inviolable law that any enemy overcome by the king in person, or by his lieutenant, was excluded from any terms at all.
So above all, of both ransom and mercy, a man should take care, if he can, of falling into the hands of a judge who is an enemy and victorious.
